'''''Regular Polytopes''''' is a [[geometry]] book on [[regular polytope]]s written by [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter]]. It was originally published by Methuen in 1947 and by Pitman Publishing in 1948,{{r|goldberg|allendoerfer|cundy|miller|walsh|frueh|wolfe|ftoth}} with a second edition published by Macmillan in 1963{{r|robinson|goldberg2|primrose|yff}} and a third edition by Dover Publications in 1973.{{r|peak|wenninger|brown}}
The Basic Library List Committee of the [[Mathematical Association of America]] has recommended that it be included in undergraduate mathematics libraries.{{r|brown}}

==Overview==
The main topics of the book are the [[Platonic solid]]s (regular convex polyhedra), related polyhedra, and their higher-dimensional generalizations.{{r|goldberg|allendoerfer}} It has 14 chapters, along with multiple appendices,{{r|cundy}} providing a more complete treatment of the subject than any earlier work, and incorporating material from 18 of Coxeter's own previous papers.{{r|goldberg}} It includes many figures (both photographs of models by Paul Donchian and drawings), tables of numerical values, and historical remarks on the subject.{{r|goldberg|allendoerfer}}

The first chapter discusses [[regular polygon]]s, regular polyhedra, basic concepts of [[graph theory]], and the [[Euler characteristic]].{{r|cundy}} Using the Euler characteristic, Coxeter derives a [[Diophantine equation]] whose [[integer]] solutions describe and classify the regular polyhedra. The second chapter uses combinations of regular polyhedra and their [[dual polyhedron|duals]] to generate related polyhedra,{{r|goldberg}} including the [[semiregular polyhedron|semiregular polyhedra]], and discusses [[zonohedron|zonohedra]] and [[Petrie polygon]]s.{{r|cundy}} Here and throughout the book, the shapes it discusses are identified and classified by their [[Schläfli symbol]]s.{{r|goldberg}} 

Chapters 3 through 5 describe the symmetries of polyhedra, first as [[permutation group]]s{{r|cundy}} and later, in the most innovative part of the book,{{r|goldberg}} as the [[Coxeter group]]s, groups generated by [[Reflection (mathematics)|reflections]] and described by the angles between their reflection planes. This part of the book also describes the regular [[tessellation]]s of the [[Euclidean plane]] and the sphere, and the regular [[Honeycomb (geometry)|honeycombs]] of [[Euclidean space]]. Chapter 6 discusses the [[Star polyhedron|star polyhedra]] including the [[Kepler–Poinsot polyhedron|Kepler–Poinsot polyhedra]].{{r|cundy}}

The remaining chapters cover higher-dimensional generalizations of these topics, including two chapters on the enumeration and construction of the [[regular polytope]]s, two chapters on higher-dimensional [[Euler characteristic]]s and background on [[quadratic form]]s, two chapters on higher-dimensional [[Coxeter group]]s, a chapter on cross-sections and projections of polytopes, and a chapter on star polytopes and [[polytope compound]]s.{{r|cundy}}

==Later editions==
The second edition was published in [[paperback]];{{r|robinson|primrose}} it adds some more recent research of [[Robert Steinberg]] on [[Petrie polygon]]s and the order of [[Coxeter group]]s,{{r|robinson|yff}} appends a new definition of polytopes at the end of the book, and makes minor corrections throughout.{{r|robinson}} The photographic plates were also enlarged for this printing,{{r|goldberg2|yff}} and some figures were redrawn.{{r|yff}} The nomenclature of these editions was occasionally cumbersome,{{r|allendoerfer}} and was modernized in the third edition. The third edition also included a new preface with added material on polyhedra in nature, found by the [[electron microscope]].{{r|peak|wenninger}}

==Reception==
The book only assumes a high-school understanding of algebra, geometry, and trigonometry,{{r|allendoerfer|cundy}} but it is primarily aimed at professionals in this area,{{r|allendoerfer}} and some steps in the book's reasoning which a professional could take for granted might be too much for less-advanced readers.{{r|cundy}} Nevertheless, reviewer J. C. P. Miller recommends it to "anyone interested in the subject, whether from recreational, educational, or other aspects",{{r|miller}} and (despite complaining about the omission of [[Regular skew polyhedron|regular skew polyhedra]]) reviewer H. E. Wolfe suggests more strongly that every mathematician should own a copy.{{r|wolfe}} Geologist A. J. Frueh Jr., describing the book as a textbook rather than a [[monograph]], suggests that the parts of the book on the symmetries of space would likely be of great interest to [[crystallography|crystallographers]]; however, Frueh complains of the lack of rigor in its proofs and the lack of clarity in its descriptions.{{r|frueh}}

Already in its first edition the book was described as "long awaited",{{r|cundy}} and "what is, and what will probably be for many years, the only organized treatment of the subject".{{r|wolfe}} In a review of the second edition, Michael Goldberg (who also reviewed the first edition){{r|goldberg}} called it "the most extensive and authoritative summary" of its area of mathematics.{{r|goldberg2}} By the time of Tricia Muldoon Brown's 2016 review, she described it as "occasionally out-of-date, although not frustratingly so", for instance in its discussion of the [[four color theorem]], proved after its last update. However, she still evaluated it as "well-written and comprehensive".{{r|brown}}
